hook.text: Foragers hunt and gather. Pastoralists herd. Farmers plow. How you get food shapes your entire society.

buildup.text: Subsistence strategies are the methods societies use to produce food and essential resources from their environment.

discovery.text: Four main types exist: foraging, pastoralism, horticulture, and intensive agriculture. Each shapes social structure.

twist.text: Foragers often work fewer hours than farmers. Agriculture brought more food but also more labor and more hierarchy.

climax.text: Subsistence is never just about food. How you produce shapes who has power, how you organize, and what you believe.

punchline.text: Tell me how you eat, and I'll describe your society.

quiz.question: What are the four main subsistence strategies?

details.summary: Subsistence strategies are the methods societies use to acquire food and basic resources — foraging, horticulture, pastoralism, intensive agriculture, and industrialism. Each strategy profoundly shapes social organization, settlement patterns, population density, and economic complexity.
details.whyItMatters: How people produce food determines nearly every aspect of their social life. Understanding subsistence strategies reveals why some societies developed states while others remained egalitarian — the link between economy and social structure is.
takeaways: Five main strategies: foraging, horticulture, pastoralism, agriculture, industrialism
Each strategy shapes social organization and settlement patterns
Food production methods fundamentally determine social complexity

faq.question: Why is foraging considered the original human economy?
faq.answer: Humans lived as foragers for roughly 95% of our species' existence. Agriculture appeared only about 10,000 years ago. Foraging societies offer insights into economic life before surplus production, social stratification, and state formation transformed human societies.

faq.question: Did the shift to agriculture improve quality of life?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. Archaeological evidence shows early farmers were shorter, sicker, and worked longer hours than foragers. Agriculture enabled population growth and social complexity but often at the cost of individual health, nutrition, and leisure.
